newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway draws up draft offshore disposal guidelines.
newsitem.headline: Norway draws up draft offshore disposal guidelines.

text.p: Norway has submitted a draft proposal for guidelines governing decommissioning of obsolete offshore oil and gas infrastructure to the intergovernmental body, OSPAR, which hopes end the debate on such disposal in September, the Energy Ministry said on Thursday.

A ministry spokesman said the proposal, drawn from discussions with individual states in the 15-membered Oslo/Paris Commission (OSPAR), was sent to OSPAR's secretariat on January 24 to be distributed to members for review.

OSPAR is an inter-governmental body monitoring and regulating pollution in the northeast Atlantic from the Arctic to Gibraltar. OSPAR signatories are Belgium, Britain, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland.
Norway has chaired the Sea Based Activity Working Group (SEBA) for decommissioning since 1995. SEBA is due to meet in France next month to try and thrash out a solution suitable to all signatories.

"This is the starting point for discussion and hopefully consensus (in OSPAR) on what to do about abandonment," the spokesman said. "The proposals are based on talks with other OSPAR members. They do not necessarily reflect the views of Norway as a member of OSPAR."
He said the document suggested two categories of installations, one where offshore disposal was banned and another for those for which dumping at sea would be one viable alternative.
Small and floating steel platforms, subsea installations and offshore loading buoys would be included in the first category.
"It all depends on weight and water depths, but this would probably included a lot of the infrastructure in the U.K. Southern Basin," he said.

For the fixed installations -- both concrete and steel, such as the Brent and Forties platforms in the British North Sea and Ekofisk, Statfjord and Gullfaks in the Norwegian North Sea, it recommends a case-by-case approach where offshore disposal could be considered.
But he added the proposal also carries an exemption clause whereby a country under exceptional circumstances could appeal against a ban to the other members.

Decommissioning and abandonment of disused offshore platforms and other installations jumped to the top of the European political agenda in 1995 when public outcry forced Shell UK to drop plans to bury the Brent Spar loading buoy in deepwaters.
Under the new proposals Brent Spar automatically fall into the banned category.

Norway and Britain, Europe's largest producers of oil and gas, have been fighting a temporary ban on offshore disposal adopted by the other OSPAR members in June, 1995 following the Brent Spar debacle. Both countries favour a case-by-case approach.
Final guidelines are expected to be agreed at OSPAR's ministerial meeting in September.
